prompt: City councils should make all public transport free of charge so that fewer people drive into city centres. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
Traffic congestion and air pollution are persistent problems in many cities, and it are tempting to believe that abolishing fares would solve them. While free public transport could persuade some motorists to leave their cars at home, I largely disagree that it should be made universally free, because the policy is costly and other measures would reduce city-center driving more effectively.

The main argument in favor of free fares is that cost is a significant factor in how people choose to travel. If a bus or train ticket costs nothing, commuters who currently drive may reconsider, particularly when they must also pay for fuel and parking. Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, introduced free travel for residents in 2013 and recorded a rise in ridership, which suggests that price can influence behavior. Free services would also benefit low-income residents, who would gained easier access to jobs and education.

Nevertheless, the policy has serious drawbacks. Fares are a major source of revenue, and without them councils would have to finance services through higher taxes or cuts elsewhere. Reduced funding often leads to overcrowded vehicles and infrequent services, which discourages the very drivers the scheme is meant to attract, moreover, evidence indicates that many new passengers are former walkers and cyclists rather than drivers, so the environmental gain is smaller than expected. Motorists tend to value convenience and comfort more than price.

A more effective strategy would combine reasonably priced, reliable public transport with measures that make driving less attractive. Congestion charges, as in London, have reduced traffic in the center while generating money that can be invested in new routes and modern vehicles. Park-and-ride facilities and dedicated bus lanes would further shorten journey times, giving commuters a practical reason to switch. Targeted discounts for students, pensioners and the unemployed could address fairness without sacrificing income.

In conclusion, althought free public transport might attract some drivers, its finance burden and limited impact make it a inefficient solution. Councils should instead invest on quality and discourage car use directly.

prompt: Some people believe that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking and managing money, while others think schools should concentrate on academic subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
People disagree about whether schools should prioritize hands-on life skills, such as preparing meals and handling personal finances, or devote their limited time mainly to traditional academic disciplines. While a strong grounding in subjects like mathematics, science, and literature remains essential, I believe schools should also teach practical competencies because these are indispensable for adult independence and are often neglected at home.

Those who favor a academically focused curriculum argue that schools exist primarily to develop intellectual ability and prepare students for higher education and skilled employment. Mastery of core subjects equips young people with analytical thinking, literacy, and numeracy, which are transferable to almost any career. Moreover, school timetables are already crowded, so adding domestic or financial instruction may reduce time available for content that are examined and formally recognized by universities. For example, a student hoping to study engineering needs advanced mathematics and physics; if those lessons were reduced, his or her future oportunities could be narrowed.

However, supporters of practical education point out that many school leavers enter adulthood without the basic knowledge required to live responsibly. Understanding budgeting, saving, debt, nutrition, and simple cooking can protected young people from serious long-term problems, including poor health and financial hardship. These skills are not inferior to academic knowledge; rather, they complement it by enabling students to apply reasoning in everyday situations, for instance, a teenager who has learned how interest rates work is far less likely to accumulate unmanageable credit-card debt, while someone who can cook several inexpensive meals is less dependent on unhealthy convenience food.

On my view, schools should maintain academic rigor while incorporating a modest but compulsory program of the life-skills education. This is especially important because not all families can teach these matters effective, and schools are the one institution that reaches nearly every child. A balanced curriculum would therefore produce graduates who are not only knowledgeable but also capable to managing real-world responsibilities. Ultimately, education should prepare students not just to pass examinations, but to lead competent, self-sufficient lives.

prompt: More and more employees now work from home for most of the week. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
The steady rise in remote work has transformed the modern labor market. Although working from home carries genuine drawbacks, I believe that its benefits for both employees and employers ultimately outweigh them, provided that organizations manage the arrangement thoughtfully.

The most compelling advantage is the improvement in time use and personal wellbeing. Commuting can consume two or three hours of a worker's day, and eliminating this journey frees time for exercise, family, or rest. A wide cited study of a Chinese travel agency, for instance, found that employees who worked remotely were not only happier but also completed more calls than thier office-based colleagues. Employers benefit as well, since reduced demand for office space lowers rent and utility costs, while a wider geographic pool of candidates makes recruitment easier.

A second advantage concerns the broader environment and society. Fewer commuters mean less traffic congestion and lower carbon emissions, wich is particularly valuable in crowded cities moreover, people who are no longer tied to expensive urban centers can settle in smaller towns, which revitalizes local economies and eases pressure on housing markets.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. Isolation is serious concern, because casual conversations in corridors often spark ideas and build trust that video calls rarely replicate. Junior staff may suffer most, since they learn by observing experienced colleagues in addition, the boundary between work and home can blur, leaving some employees answering messages late at night and struggling to switch off, which may eventually lead at burnout.

However, these problems are largely solvable. Companies can requiring occasional days in the office for collaboration, establish clear expectations about working hours, and organize mentoring schemes for newcomers. Such measures preserve the society fabric of the workplace without sacrificing flexibility.

In conclusion, remote work offers substantial gains in productivity, cost savings, and quality of the life, while its main weaknesses can be mitigated through sensible policies. On balance, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.
